_comment: Pass/fail bars for a qualification run (#119). DECLARED BEFORE RUNNING, on purpose.
The issue's sharpest instruction is 'avoid moving the threshold after seeing the result'. That
is unenforceable as advice, so it is enforced instead: every result records the sha256 of this
file, and scripts/verify_capacity_claims.py refuses a capacity claim whose cited run was judged
against a different version of it. Loosening a bar to turn a red run green therefore
invalidates the claim it was loosened for, and the profile has to be re-run.
Only metrics that EVERY qualification scenario measures are gated. A metric the harness cannot
observe is reported as unmeasured, and a threshold over an unmeasured metric fails rather than
passing quietly — so adding a bar here for something nothing measures breaks every run, which
is the correct outcome and not a reason to soften the rule.

CHANGE LOG. 1.1.0: `api_5xx_rate` and `api_seconds_p95` were REDEFINED (not re-valued) to cover the control plane only, after the first smoke run showed the 2 s bar failing snapshots that the same file separately allows 10 s. A threshold set that grades one call against two contradictory bars is broken, so the definition was fixed and the version moved — which invalidates any claim citing 1.0.0, exactly as intended. No bar was loosened: every VALUE here is unchanged from the set declared before the first run.

thresholds.why: 30 s/camera-hour is 99.2% coverage. Gaps the harness itself caused by unplugging a publisher are subtracted; what remains is coverage the recorder lost on its own, which is the number a retention or evidence claim rests on.
A segment that indexes but will not decode is worse than a missing one: the timeline says the footage exists. Zero, not a rate — one unplayable segment is one piece of evidence that is not there.
A camera that drops must be back within a minute at P95, or a fleet with ordinary network churn accumulates gaps faster than the coverage bar allows.
Recovery is every camera recording again, not the API answering. Two minutes is an upgrade window an operator can accept; longer and a routine restart becomes a scheduled outage.
Live view is the most-used operator path. One failure in a hundred is already noticeable at a video wall refreshing every few seconds.
Beyond five seconds to hand back a live URL, an operator assumes the camera is down and starts investigating a system that is working.
Snapshots contend with the recorder for the same stream, so a slightly looser bar than live view — but a failing snapshot is a failing thumbnail everywhere in the dashboard.
A snapshot must wait for a keyframe; ten seconds covers a two-second GOP with contention and still fails a box that is genuinely saturated.
Clip export is the evidence path. Windows with no footage are excluded from the rate (a 404 is a fact about the window); what is graded is whether existing footage could be exported.
A 30-second clip is `-c copy`, so it is a concat and a trim. If P95 exceeds 30 s the disk, not the encoder, is the limit — and that is a capacity finding.

Counts connection failures as well as 5xx, over CONTROL-PLANE calls: snapshot, live view and clip have their own bars below. Calls to a camera the harness has deliberately unplugged are excluded; calls to any other camera are not. This is the externally visible superset of SQLite contention, which the kernel exposes no counter for.

Control-plane calls only — the dashboard makes several per view, and a two-second P95 is already a sluggish page. Media paths are measured separately because a snapshot must wait for a keyframe and cannot be held to a control-plane bar.
